doc.title: Billie Pierce and De De Pierce Interview, 1959-04-02

chapter: De De's career and trumpet players
title: Chris Kelly the blues man, mutes and high-note trumpeters
summary: De De describes Chris Kelly as strictly a blues man whose playing could start fights, his plunger and tin-can mutes, and Albert Glenny working with him and Rene. Asked about high-note men, De De names Louis DeMaine.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Chris Kelly, the blues trumpeter and his band

blocks.x: Did you hear Chris Kelly? Oh yeah, I knew Chris. Did you play with him and him?
I knew Chris, well I have worked with him often on little jobs too.
How was his style?
How was that his style, huh?
How did he play?

Blues, strictly blues man. Nothing but blues. He was known to play more blues than any man in the city. He was known for that. He was known that Chris Kelly, if he wanted to- He was known for this one.
Okay, we got it going again. You're talking about Mr. Chris Kelly?

Chris Kelly, yeah. He was known as one of the greatest blues players that I ever known. It was known, it has been proven, that Chris Kelly, as though he was playing a dance, he could play a blues and otherwise start a general fight over the music, the blues, and break up a dance. He'd known he could do that, make disagreement among the dancers. He played those blues, it was such a feeling. He got people to go to fight in the place. He was known for that. Strictly a blues man. Of course I played alongside him a long time, off and on, different jobs, he'd hire me.
Did he use a lot of mutes?
Yeah a lot of wah-wah, most of the wah-wah. In other words one of those rubber wah-wahs Yeah, for the flushes, yeah. One of those.
Did he use a mute inside the horn in that too?
No, no, no. Just the flushing? No, the varicellum used it. But open? Open, even with a tin can, a tomato can, anything, a milk can, anything. Take a can and do just as well. I mean today, you know.
Did Buddy Petit use those things too like that?
Buddy another one, yeah. Beer can, anything, in the way of speaking. Any old tin can, something like that, for a mute.
What about Kid Rene? Did he play much open horn or with mutes too?
Mostly open, mostly wide open all the time. Varicellum used the rubber, you know. Varicellum. But he's only fast fingering, finger fast.
When you played with Chris or heard him play, who else was in the band, can you remember? Ooh. Anybody else at all? I know you had all of them, but some of them maybe.

One of, how do you call it? Even old Glenny had worked with him off and on too. Oh, Albert Glenny. He's worked with him and Rene too, worked with both of the bands off and on, you know. That's what they used to do. Alternate in other words, you know. And one had more work than the other, well they'd work with him and the fellow had the most work, they'd work with them. That's where they used to go at the time.
Who was the highest note man around here at that time?
I don't remember.
Was anybody specialized in playing higher parts than others?
DeMaine was pretty fair, Louis DeMaine.
Louis DeMaine.
In his time, yeah.
Was, did Buddy Petit play as high as Kidman A?
No, but it, no, no, no, Buddy was my 200. You didn't? I wouldn't call him no high note man, no, no, no.
